everything: Your role is also called this, but your headline does not say so: "Software Engineer" (40%), "Python Developer" (12%). Recruiters and ATS search by role title. Fix your LinkedIn headline (people find you by it) and the base PDFs, for example: "Senior Backend / Software Engineer | Python · PostgreSQL · …". The "📄 CV" button already does this: the headline follows the vacancy title.

Frequent, but different roles: "AI Engineer" (20%), "Full Stack" (15%). No need to rename yourself. If you have related experience (for example, RAG / LLM for AI roles), you can apply to backend positions in such teams: the CV generator puts an LLM / RAG headline for AI vacancies.
In the cv/base.toml base, but not in the PDF CV: Kafka (30%) — rebuild the base CVs (cvgen.py --base …).
Gaps — often required, but missing from the CV: Go (25%). This is about experience, not wording: if you have it — add it to the base, if not — these are candidates to learn.
The PDF CV is longer than one page (Backend). For the Western market with 6 years of experience one page is better — the "1 page" button in the report and on the CV page builds it.
Words that make the CV sound like a list of duties or like AI: "responsible for", "leveraged" — replace them with a concrete action and result.
All bullets have one form: 9 of 10 start with a past-tense verb. Sameness gives away a template (and AI) — start some bullets with the result or the problem, add a couple of short ones.

Numbers in almost every bullet: Globex (6) bullets with numbers. A measurable result is strong, but numbers everywhere can look inflated: keep the weightiest, and in the rest show the scale or who uses it. (Opinions differ: some advice says "numbers everywhere", some "no more than two or three per workplace".)
Long bullets (more than 45 words): 2 — readers spend 5 seconds on them, one idea per bullet is better.
